title: Setting Up a New Router (NZ Fibre)
cardText: Set up a new or replacement router on a New Zealand fibre broadband connection.
Connect the router to the fibre ONT and configure the correct ISP WAN settings.
Check DHCP, PPPoE, VLAN tagging, Wi-Fi and internet connectivity.
text: This guide explains how to install a new or replacement router on a New Zealand fibre broadband connection.
You will need the router, its power adapter, an Ethernet cable and access to the fibre ONT.
The ONT is the fibre connection box usually mounted on a wall.
Most NZ fibre providers use VLAN 10, but WAN authentication and VLAN requirements differ between providers.
Use your own ISP's published settings rather than assuming every fibre connection is the same.
This guide is for standard fibre connections using an Ethernet WAN port. Mobile broadband, DSL and some Hyperfibre installations may require different equipment.

checkServiceActive.title: Is the fibre broadband service active?
body: Confirm that the internet provider has activated the fibre service at the property.
Check the activation email or account information if the service is new.
Make sure the fibre ONT is powered on and does not show an optical fault.
If the service has not been activated, router configuration alone will not establish an internet connection.

confirmActivation.title: Confirm fibre activation
body: Contact the internet provider to confirm that the fibre service is active.
Ask which ONT Ethernet port is assigned to the broadband service.
If the ONT displays an optical fault, report the indicator lights to the provider.
Continue with router setup once the service is confirmed active.

checkRouterCompatibility.title: Check that the router supports fibre broadband
body: Check that the router has an Ethernet WAN or Internet port.
Confirm that it supports the WAN connection type required by the provider, usually DHCP/IPoE or PPPoE.
Check whether it supports 802.1Q VLAN tagging if the ISP requires it.
A router that only supports an ADSL or VDSL telephone connection may not be suitable unless it also has an Ethernet WAN mode.
Check that the router supports the speed of the broadband plan.
Some ISP-supplied routers may have restricted or locked configuration settings.

routerNotCompatible.title: Router may not be compatible
body: The router does not appear to support the required fibre WAN connection.
Check the manufacturer's specifications for Ethernet WAN, DHCP, PPPoE and VLAN support.
If the provider requires VLAN tagging and the router cannot configure it, use another compatible router.
For Hyperfibre plans, check whether faster Ethernet ports or special equipment are required.

connectRouterToOnt.title: Connect the router to the fibre ONT
body: Place the router near the ONT or an existing Ethernet connection leading to it.
Connect an Ethernet cable from the activated LAN port on the ONT to the WAN or Internet port on the router.
Check the provider's activation information for the correct ONT port. Do not assume it is always LAN1.
Connect the router's power adapter and switch it on.
Wait for the router to complete its startup process.
Do not disconnect the fibre-optic cable or press the ONT factory Reset button.
connectRouterToOnt.alt: Ethernet cable connected to a router WAN port
connectRouterToOnt.caption: Example router WAN port connection. The ONT connects to the router's WAN or Internet port.

link.name: One NZ: Set up your own modem
link.description: Official NZ instructions showing how to connect a compatible router to a fibre ONT.

connectionProblem.title: Check the physical connection
body: Check that the Ethernet cable connects the active ONT LAN port to the router's WAN port.
Try another known-working Ethernet cable if available.
Confirm the router is powered on and that the ONT is showing its normal service indicators.
If the required ONT port or router WAN connection is unclear, consult the ISP or router manual.

loginRouter.title: Log in to the router
body: Connect a computer to one of the router's LAN ports or its default Wi-Fi network.
The default Wi-Fi name, password and administration address are often printed on the router label.
Open a web browser and enter the router's administration address.
Common examples are 192.168.1.1 and 192.168.0.1, but the correct address depends on the router.
On Windows, open Command Prompt and run ipconfig to find the Default Gateway address if necessary.
Sign in using the router's administration credentials.
If it is a new router, follow the initial setup wizard and create an administrator password when prompted.

routerLoginProblem.title: Cannot access router settings
body: Confirm the computer is connected to the new router rather than another nearby Wi-Fi network.
Check the router label or manufacturer instructions for the correct administration address.
Use ipconfig to check the Default Gateway on Windows.
Try a direct Ethernet connection if Wi-Fi access is not working.
Use the router's documented login or password-recovery procedure if required.
Only factory-reset the router if you understand that existing settings will be lost.

checkIspSettings.title: Find the correct NZ internet provider settings
body: Identify the customer's internet service provider.
Use the relevant official support link below to check the provider's fibre WAN settings.
Check whether the provider requires DHCP/IPoE or PPPoE.
Check whether 802.1Q VLAN tagging is required, including the VLAN ID and priority.
Many NZ fibre providers use VLAN ID 10 and priority 0, but this is not universal.
For example, Spark uses PPPoE and VLAN 10, while 2degrees uses DHCP and VLAN 10.
Skinny's published BYO fibre settings use PPPoE with VLAN tagging disabled.
Confirm any required username and password before proceeding.

confirmIspSettings.title: Confirm router settings with the ISP
body: Do not guess the internet provider's connection settings.
Contact the ISP and confirm the WAN connection type, VLAN requirements and any authentication details.
Ask whether the service supports a third-party router.
Once the settings are confirmed, continue the router installation.

configureWan.title: Configure the router WAN connection
body: Open the Internet, WAN or Quick Setup section of the router.
Select the connection type required by the customer's ISP.
For DHCP/IPoE, select Dynamic IP, Automatic IP or the equivalent option.
For PPPoE, select PPPoE and enter the username and password required by the ISP.
Do not use PPPoE simply because the router offers it as an option.
Leave DNS settings on Automatic unless the provider requires otherwise.
Save the settings and allow the router to establish the internet connection.
configureWan.alt: Router administration screen showing Dynamic IP and PPPoE WAN connection choices
configureWan.caption: Example TP-Link WAN settings. Choose the connection type required by your ISP.

routerSettingsProblem.title: Router settings unavailable
body: The required WAN connection settings cannot be configured on the router.
Check whether the router has a Quick Setup wizard, Advanced settings or a separate Internet configuration page.
Consult the manufacturer's instructions for your exact router model.
If the firmware is restricted or the required settings are unsupported, use a compatible router.

configureVlan.title: Configure VLAN tagging if required
body: Check whether the internet provider requires VLAN tagging.
If required, find the Internet VLAN, IPTV/VLAN, 802.1Q or ISP Profile settings.
Enable 802.1Q tagging and enter the provider's VLAN ID.
For providers requiring VLAN 10 and priority 0, enter Internet VLAN ID 10 and VLAN Priority 0.
Some routers have a preset ISP profile or New Zealand UFB option.
If the provider requires an untagged connection, leave VLAN tagging disabled.
Do not change IPTV or VoIP VLAN settings unless the provider has supplied those values.
Save the settings and allow the router to reconnect.
configureVlan.alt: TP-Link router VLAN configuration screen showing Internet VLAN ID and priority settings
configureVlan.caption: Example TP-Link VLAN configuration. The screenshot uses VLAN 100 for illustration; enter your ISP's actual value, commonly 10 for NZ fibre.

link.name: TP-Link: Set up VLAN ID
link.description: Official instructions showing where to configure Internet VLAN ID and priority on supported TP-Link routers.

checkWanConnection.title: Check whether the router has internet access
body: Open the router's Internet Status or WAN Status page.
Check whether the connection is reported as Connected.
For DHCP connections, check whether the router has received a WAN IP address.
For PPPoE connections, check whether the session has authenticated successfully.
A private or CGNAT WAN address can be normal and does not necessarily indicate a fault.
If the router reports Disconnected or Authentication Failed, continue troubleshooting.

checkWanProblem.title: Check why the WAN connection failed
body: Check that the Ethernet cable is connected to the router's WAN port and the correct ONT port.
Confirm the ISP service is active and the ONT lights are normal.
Review the selected DHCP or PPPoE connection type.
Check any PPPoE username and password.
Verify VLAN tagging, VLAN ID and priority against the ISP's published requirements.
Restart the router after saving confirmed settings if necessary.
If the connection still fails, contact the ISP and ask them to check the service and ONT port provisioning.

setupWifi.title: Configure the router Wi-Fi network
body: Open the Wireless or Wi-Fi settings in the router.
Choose a Wi-Fi network name (SSID) and a strong password.
Use WPA2-AES or WPA3 security where supported by your devices.
If replacing an existing router, you may reuse the previous Wi-Fi name and password to help existing devices reconnect.
Check whether the router combines 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks or configures them separately.
Save the wireless settings.
If you changed the Wi-Fi name or password, reconnect your computer or phone using the new details.

wifiSetupProblem.title: Wi-Fi configuration problem
body: Check whether the router's wireless function is enabled.
Review the Wi-Fi name, security mode and password.
If possible, connect a computer using Ethernet to access the router settings.
Consult the router manufacturer's setup instructions if wireless settings cannot be saved.

testInternet.title: Test the internet connection
body: Connect a computer or phone to the new router.
Open several websites to confirm internet access.
Test both Wi-Fi and Ethernet if possible.
Check that the router remains connected after a restart.
If the router has internet access but one device does not, troubleshoot that device's local connection.

testConnectionProblem.title: Is the router WAN connection still active?
body: Check the router's WAN or Internet Status page again.
If the WAN is connected, investigate the affected device, Wi-Fi connection, DNS or other local settings.
If the WAN has disconnected, review the physical connection and ISP settings.
Use the No Internet Connection troubleshooting guide for more detailed diagnostics.

localConnectionProblem.title: Check local network connectivity
body: The router reports a working WAN connection, but internet access still fails on a connected device.
Check that the device receives an IP address, default gateway and DNS settings.
Try another device or an Ethernet connection to isolate Wi-Fi problems.
Continue with the No Internet Connection guide if the problem remains.

routerSetupComplete.title: Router setup complete
body: The new router is connected to the fibre service and internet access is working.
Confirm that the Wi-Fi network and password are correct.
Reconnect household devices as required.
Keep a record of the router model, administration address and relevant ISP WAN settings.
Check for manufacturer firmware updates and save a configuration backup if the router supports it.
If the customer uses an internet phone service, confirm that calling also works.

contactIsp.title: Contact the internet provider
body: The router has not established a working internet connection.
Record the router model, ONT status lights and the exact WAN connection error.
Tell the ISP which WAN protocol and VLAN settings have been configured.
Ask the ISP to confirm service activation, the correct ONT port, connection authentication and BYO-router compatibility.
If the service includes voice calling, confirm whether the provider requires its own equipment.
